definition: Topography means the arrangement of an area's physical features, especially its elevation and shape.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word topography. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know topography should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The valley's topography funnels every storm into one narrow gap, which is why the town at the mouth floods.
Layout is a loose word for how anything is arranged, while topography is specifically the arrangement of a landscape's physical surface.
Relief is narrower and more technical than topography, naming elevation differences alone, while topography takes in ridges, valleys, rivers, and slopes together.

Terrain is the ground considered as something to move across -- soldiers and hikers judge terrain rough or easy going. Topography is the ground considered as something to measure and map: the arrangement of an area's elevations and shapes, whether or not anyone crosses it.

The lie of the land is the plain-spoken phrase for how ground rises, falls, and drains -- what a farmer reads on an afternoon's walk. Topography is the surveyor's term for the same thing set down precisely: an area's shape and elevation, measured and mapped.

Two neighbouring farms receive the same rainfall and grow the same wheat, yet one loses topsoil every spring and the other does not.
A surveyor walking both fields explains the difference in an afternoon: the first farm's ground tilts eight degrees toward a single gully, while the second's lies almost flat behind a low ridge.
Nothing about the soil or the seed differs between them.
The whole difference is topography.
With the same soil, the same seed, and the same rain, the only difference between the farms is the slope and shape of the ground, which is exactly what topography describes.
Topography names the ground itself and normally takes 'the ...

of': the topography of the basin, rather than 'a topography.' It covers shape and elevation only, since climate, soil, and plant life are separate matters, and mountainous country is one kind of topography rather than a synonym for the word.

When Linville hired its first bicycle planner, she did not begin with traffic counts.
She began with a contour map, because the city's topography would decide everything else.
Three steep ridges wall in the eastern neighborhoods, and a single low saddle carries every road that leaves town to the west.
On paper, the shortest route from the mill district to downtown ran straight over the highest ridge.
Legs, unlike lines on paper, must climb.
So the planner traced the valley floors instead, letting her routes follow the flat ground beside the creeks, adding distance but sparing riders the steepest grades.
Her final network looked nothing like the road grid above it.
It looked like the land itself: a map of where the hills allowed people to go.
